units.title: Unit 07 — Intensifying and softening adverbs
learningObjectives: Distinguish intensifying adverbs from softening adverbs and interpret their effect on the strength of an adjective or verb.
Choose natural restricted combinations such as greatly appreciate, strongly influence, highly recommended and absolutely delighted.
Interpret the register of emphatic and understated phrases, including informal dead easy and more formal faintly ridiculous.

items.example: Several viewers found the comedian's comments deeply offensive.
items.note: Deeply strengthens a negative judgement of offence, not physical depth.

items.example: The rented apartment was spotlessly clean when we arrived.
items.note: Spotlessly signals that no dirt or marks are visible; especially natural for places and surfaces.

items.example: Ignoring the host throughout dinner was downright rude.
items.note: Downright emphasises an unpleasant quality in a forceful, conversational way.

items.example: After blaming the wrong colleague, he felt thoroughly ashamed.
items.note: Thoroughly marks a complete or intense feeling of shame.

items.example: It was blatantly obvious that the figures had been manipulated.
items.note: Blatantly adds a strong suggestion that the fact is plain to see.

items.example: The advertising claims were wildly exaggerated and misled several buyers.
items.note: Wildly signals extreme exaggeration beyond what the facts support.

items.example: The instructions looked complicated, but the setup was dead easy.
items.note: Dead is a very informal British English intensifier with easy.

items.example: The initial estimate proved wildly inaccurate after the final measurements.
items.note: Wildly inaccurate describes a very large departure from the truth or correct value.

items.example: I really enjoy the quiet hours before the office opens.
items.note: Really intensifies an enjoyment verb naturally without changing its register.

items.example: One phrase in the report was slightly offensive, though the rest was respectful.
items.note: Slightly reduces the strength of offensive and conveys a limited degree.

items.example: The revised timetable is slightly different from the one we discussed.
items.note: Slightly is a flexible softener and commonly modifies comparative qualities.

items.example: I was mildly surprised when the team finished a day ahead of schedule.
items.note: Mildly signals a restrained reaction, less intense than genuinely shocked.

items.example: The examiner seemed mildly amused by the unusual answer.
items.note: Mildly often combines with emotional reaction adjectives and participles.

items.example: She was mildly irritated by the repeated notifications.
items.note: Mildly reduces the severity of irritation and avoids exaggeration.

items.example: The joke may sound mildly offensive to some listeners.
items.note: Mildly indicates that the perceived offence is limited in degree.

items.example: The miniseries is loosely based on events from the explorer's life.
items.note: Loosely based on acknowledges inspiration without claiming close fidelity.

items.example: The workshop was loosely structured so participants could explore their own ideas.
items.note: Loosely describes a flexible structure rather than a carefully fixed sequence.

items.example: The second chapter addresses a loosely related issue.
items.note: Loosely related signals a weak or indirect connection.

items.example: The interviews covered several loosely connected themes.
items.note: Loosely connected describes a connection without a tight organisation or link.

items.example: The proposal sounded faintly ridiculous until she explained its purpose.
items.note: Faintly is a fairly formal softener conveying a slight impression.

items.example: The professor looked faintly amused by the student's creative excuse.
items.note: Faintly suggests only a small visible degree of amusement.

items.example: He appeared faintly surprised that anyone remembered the incident.
items.note: Faintly tones down the degree of surprise; it is more formal than a bit.

items.example: Her explanation sounded faintly absurd, but we listened carefully.
items.note: Faintly absurd expresses a mild judgement in relatively formal language.

items.example: It is highly unlikely that the missing records will be recovered intact.
items.note: Highly works with unlikely, but it cannot freely replace very before every adjective.

items.example: The organisation recruits highly educated specialists from several fields.
items.note: Highly naturally modifies educated and other adjectives of degree or status.

items.example: This short guide is highly recommended for new volunteers.
items.note: Highly recommended is idiomatic for a strong endorsement.

items.example: Early experiences strongly influence how children learn to trust others.
items.note: Strongly collocates with influence, unlike highly in this verb sense.

items.example: We greatly appreciate the support offered by local residents.
items.note: Greatly, rather than strongly, is the idiomatic adverb with appreciate.

items.example: The change in regulations could greatly influence investment decisions.
items.note: Greatly is a natural alternative to strongly with influence.

items.example: The suggestion that everyone should work without sleep was utterly absurd.
items.note: Utterly combines naturally with strong negative adjectives such as absurd.

items.example: Charging an entry fee for a public footpath seems utterly ridiculous.
items.note: Utterly highlights the extreme nature of a strong evaluative adjective.

items.example: The final design is completely different from the early sketches.
items.note: Completely stresses total rather than minor difference.

items.example: The remote station is totally dependent on satellite communications.
items.note: Totally dependent is a natural strong combination for complete reliance.

items.example: The training budget is entirely separate from the equipment budget.
items.note: Entirely emphasises that two things do not overlap or connect.

items.example: We thoroughly enjoyed the performance despite the rainy weather.
items.note: Thoroughly is especially natural with enjoy, but not interchangeable with every intensifier.

items.example: The graduates were absolutely delighted with the scholarship announcement.
items.note: Absolutely generally favours extreme or non-gradable adjectives such as delighted.

items.example: The children were very happy with their handmade presents.
items.note: Very happy is natural; absolutely happy is not the standard pairing taught for this meaning.

items.example: His response sounded faintly patronising even though he intended to help.
items.note: Faintly can reduce the strength of this relatively formal criticism.

items.example: The colour scheme looked mildly ridiculous in the bright sunlight.
items.note: Mildly is an alternative softener for ridiculous in suitable contexts.

items.example: The last stage of the climb was incredibly difficult in the heat.
items.note: Incredibly is a widely usable intensifier before adjectives such as difficult.

items.example: It was awfully sweet of you to remember my birthday.
items.note: Awfully can strengthen a positive adjective in conversational English.

items.example: He felt terribly lonely after moving to a city where he knew no one.
items.note: Terribly intensifies lonely and is not restricted to negative events.

items.example: The clinic has been extremely busy since the holiday weekend.
items.note: Extremely is a flexible degree adverb that pairs naturally with busy.

items.example: The hotel was terribly expensive during the music festival.
items.note: Terribly can intensify expensive, especially in conversational language.

items.example: The application is completely dependent on a stable internet connection.
items.note: Completely dependent is another natural choice for total reliance.

items.example: Her style was strongly influenced by the artists she studied.
items.note: The passive participle influenced naturally takes strongly, not highly.

items.example: Your constructive feedback is greatly appreciated by the entire team.
items.note: Greatly appreciated is the idiomatic passive form in polite acknowledgements.

units.title: Unit 08 — Make and verbs that mean make
learningObjectives: Use make with conventional noun partners while avoiding errors involving do, give and have.
Apply extended make expressions for proposals, discoveries, habits, attempts, offers and opposition in original contexts.
Select more or less formal alternatives to make such as create, stage, lodge, rustle up, run up, turn and coin.

items.example: Please make suggestions before we finalise the event programme.
items.note: Make, rather than do or give, is the standard verb with suggestions.

items.example: Every volunteer can make a contribution to the neighbourhood project.
items.note: Make a contribution is idiomatic for adding value, money, effort or an idea.

items.pt: apresentar um pedido formal de desculpas
items.example: The director agreed to make a formal apology after the incident.
items.note: Make an apology, not give an apology, is the usual standard combination.

items.example: We need to make improvements to the booking process before launch.
items.note: Make is idiomatic with improvements, rather than do improvements.

items.example: The coordinator will make arrangements for the speakers' accommodation.
items.note: Make arrangements refers to organising practical details in advance.

items.example: Our neighbours plan to have a party after the renovation ends.
items.note: Have a party is idiomatic; make a party is not a natural standard alternative.

items.example: She hopes to do research on urban transport after graduating.
items.note: Do research is usual in this context, rather than make research.

items.example: I try to make a habit of reviewing new vocabulary each evening.
items.note: Use make a habit of followed by a noun or an -ing form.

items.example: A manager who humiliates colleagues is likely to make enemies.
items.note: Make enemies means cause others to dislike or oppose you.

items.example: She decided to make an attempt to restore the damaged painting.
items.note: Make an attempt commonly takes to plus infinitive to specify the action.

items.example: With careful planning, they could make a success of the community café.
items.note: Make a success of something means manage it effectively enough to succeed.

items.example: We decided to make an early escape before the speeches began.
items.note: Make an early escape means leave an occasion early, often discreetly.

items.example: The archaeologists hope to make a discovery that changes the dating of the site.
items.note: Make a discovery is the conventional collocation for finding something previously unknown.

items.example: The students must make calculations before choosing the correct material.
items.note: Make calculations refers to computing results; the phrase is common in technical contexts.

items.example: We moved the shelves to make room for another desk.
items.note: Make room for means free physical space or allow something new into a plan.

items.example: I was pleased to make the ambassador's acquaintance at the reception.
items.note: Make someone's acquaintance is a relatively formal way to say meet someone.

items.example: The couple decided to make an offer on the apartment after the second viewing.
items.note: Make an offer on is particularly natural when discussing property purchases.

items.example: The committee will make a proposal at next month's meeting.
items.note: Make a proposal is a formal way to present a suggested course of action.

items.example: Local residents chose to make a stand against the closure of the library.
items.note: Make a stand against means actively resist or publicly oppose something.

items.example: Clear explanations can create a good impression during an interview.
items.note: Create an impression is somewhat more formal than make an impression.

items.example: Soft lighting can create an atmosphere of calm in the waiting room.
items.note: Create an atmosphere is somewhat more formal than make for an atmosphere.

items.example: Students plan to stage a protest against the proposed fee increase.
items.note: Stage a protest is a standard, relatively formal alternative to make a protest.

items.example: Several passengers decided to lodge a complaint with the transport authority.
items.note: Lodge a complaint is formal and suits official complaints procedures.

items.example: We managed to rustle up a meal from the vegetables left in the fridge.
items.note: Rustle up is informal and suggests preparing something quickly with what is available.

items.example: She offered to run up curtains for the new studio in one afternoon.
items.note: Run up can mean make something quickly using a sewing machine; the expression is informal.

items.example: After two years of losses, the small company finally began to turn a profit.
items.note: Turn a profit is less formal than make a profit and means become profitable.

items.example: The journalist helped coin a phrase that later became widely used.
items.note: Coin a phrase means invent a new expression, not merely quote one.

items.example: The organisers had to make changes to the schedule at short notice.
items.note: Make changes is the usual collocation for altering a procedure, design or plan.

items.example: Arriving prepared can help applicants make a good first impression.
items.note: Make a good first impression is a natural alternative to the more formal create.

items.example: The shop hopes to make a profit once the initial costs are covered.
items.note: Make a profit is the ordinary neutral alternative to turn a profit.

items.example: We may need to make a formal complaint if the problem is not resolved.
items.note: Make a formal complaint is neutral to formal; lodge a complaint sounds more official.

items.example: The rescue team had to make several attempts to reach the stranded hikers.
items.note: The plural form several attempts is common for repeated efforts to achieve a goal.

items.example: The new intern has already made a positive contribution to the team's work.
items.note: Make a positive contribution builds on the established make a contribution pattern.

items.example: You should make an effort to practise the phrases in conversation.
items.note: Make an effort is followed naturally by to plus infinitive.

items.example: Our supervisor makes a point of thanking everyone who helps.
items.note: Make a point of means deliberately and consistently ensure you do something.

items.example: Learners will make mistakes when trying unfamiliar expressions.
items.note: Make mistakes, not do mistakes, is the idiomatic combination.

items.example: The guests hoped to make an escape before the reception became crowded.
items.note: Make an escape suggests finding a way to leave, sometimes without attention.

items.example: The team made an important discovery while studying the cave paintings.
items.note: This is a natural expansion of make a discovery with an adjective.
